newsitem.title: USA: US-Japan insurance talks seen headed for showdown.
newsitem.headline: US-Japan insurance talks seen headed for showdown.

text.p: U.S. trade negotiator Ira Shapiro said on Saturday talks to open up Japan's giant insurance market would likely have to be carried over to the ministerial level for a showdown before the Dec. 15 deadline.
"I hope (Eisuke) Sakakibara and I will resolve everything, but the odds are that won't happen," Shapiro told reporters during a break in the San Francisco talks.

Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, Shapiro and other trade negotiators resumed their two-day talks on Saturday in a race to settle their differences ahead of the Dec. 15 deadline.
At the end of their morning session, negotiators exchanged documents and went into different rooms to review the papers.
"We've done some work to clarify some things we had already, and we've just exchanged some ideas on that," Shapiro said. "I wouldn't call it new proposals."
Sakakibara said earlier that Dec. 15 remained Tokyo's target, but he described the San Francisco talks thus far as "rough sailing."

Sakakibara said he wanted to set up a ministerial-level meeting, although he did not say when the proposed meeting could be held. Sakakibara said he would at a minimum like to set a timetable for the final negotiations.

At issue is Japan's $382 billion domestic insurance market. Washington is pressing Japan to liberalize its primary insurance markets before a niche area called the "Third Sector," where U.S. firms have been dominant, is opened up to Japanese insurers.
The Third Sector includes areas such as personal accident, illness and nursing care, and stand-alone cancer policies.

The dispute has become a major trade irritant between the two countries. They had originally set a July 31 deadline to settle the dispute, but recently agreed to push the deadline to reach an agreement to Dec. 15.
Negotiators meeting in San Francisco have declined to discuss details of the ongoing talks.
Late on Friday, Shapiro told reporters major differences between the two sides remained. "We've had a good meeting, but differences are still significant," he said.
Sakakibara said he expected no quick breakthrough.

The United States wants Japan to live up to a 1994 agreement that called for deregulation of the primary sector dominated by big Japanese firms before deregulation of the so-called third sector of specialty insurance.

On Thursday, a U.S. trade official in Washington expressed doubt the dispute would be fully resolved in these talks. He said the "ball is substantially in Japan's court" because Tokyo removed a number of primary sector issues from the table during negotiations in September.
